title: Roadmap 07: DSA intervals, bits, DP and backtracking
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: Intervals and scheduling, bit tricks, dynamic programming (state, transition, base case), when greedy works, backtracking complexity, and habits for timed mock interviews.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: Given meeting intervals, you need the minimum number of rooms. After sorting meetings by start time, which structure tells you when a room frees up?

options.text: A max-heap of start times, always reusing the newest room.
options.why: Start times do not say when a room becomes free.

options.text: A stack of intervals, popped whenever two intervals overlap.
options.why: A stack loses the earliest finishing time needed for reuse.

options.text: A hash set of room numbers keyed by each meeting's start time.
options.why: A set cannot tell you which room finishes first.

options.text: A min-heap of end times, popped when the next start is later.
options.why: Right: the heap size at the end is the rooms needed, in O(n log n).

questions.explanation: Each meeting either reuses the room that frees up earliest or needs a new one. A sweep line over sorted start and end events gives the same answer. Merge intervals also starts by sorting on start.

questions.prompt: To keep the largest possible number of non-overlapping intervals, which greedy choice is provably correct?

options.text: Sort by start time and take the earliest-starting interval that fits.
options.why: A very long early interval can block many short ones.

options.text: Sort by end time and take each interval that fits after the last one.
options.why: Right: finishing earliest leaves the most room for the rest.

options.text: Always take the shortest interval that does not overlap the chosen ones.
options.why: A short interval in the middle can block two longer, compatible ones.

options.text: Always take the interval that overlaps the fewest other intervals.
options.why: This heuristic has counterexamples and no exchange-argument proof.

questions.explanation: Exchange argument: in any optimal answer you can swap the first interval for the one with the earliest end without losing count, so the greedy choice is safe.

questions.prompt: Select all statements about bit tricks that are true.

options.text: n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit, so for n > 0 a result of 0 means n is a power of two.
options.why: Right: a power of two has exactly one set bit.

options.text: If every other value appears exactly twice, XOR-ing all values leaves the one that appears once.
options.why: Right: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, and XOR is commutative.

options.text: For a /24 prefix the mask is 255.255.255.0, and ip & mask gives the network address.
options.why: Right: the first 24 bits are kept and the host bits become 0.

options.text: x ^ x equals x, so XOR-ing a value with itself leaves it unchanged.
options.why: x ^ x is 0, and that is exactly why paired values cancel.

questions.explanation: The same ideas give popcount (loop n &= n - 1), and checking whether an address is inside a subnet: (ip & mask) == (network & mask).

questions.prompt: In edit distance, dp[i][j] is the minimum number of inserts, deletes or replaces to turn the first i characters of a into the first j characters of b. What are the correct base cases?

options.text: dp[i][0] = 0 and dp[0][j] = 0, since an empty string costs nothing.
options.why: Turning "abc" into "" needs 3 deletes, not 0.

options.text: dp[i][0] = 1 and dp[0][j] = 1, because one operation is always needed.
options.why: The cost grows with the length: i deletes or j inserts.

options.text: dp[0][0] = 1 and every other cell in the first row and column is 0.
options.why: dp[0][0] is 0: two empty strings already match.

options.text: dp[i][0] = i (i deletes) and dp[0][j] = j (j inserts).
options.why: Right: converting to or from the empty string costs its length.

questions.explanation: Transition: if a[i-1] == b[j-1] then dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1], else 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]). Always state the state, transition and base case aloud. Time and space are O(m * n).

questions.prompt: True or false: for any coin system, repeatedly taking the largest coin that fits gives the fewest coins. Example: coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6.

options.text: True
options.why: That would make coin change a greedy problem for every set of coins.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: greedy gives 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins, but 3 + 3 = 2 coins is better.

questions.explanation: Greedy needs a proof (an exchange argument) or a known structure such as canonical coin systems. When a counterexample exists, use DP: dp[x] = 1 + min(dp[x - c]) over coins c, with dp[0] = 0.

questions.prompt: True or false: top-down memoization only computes the subproblems that the recursion actually reaches, while bottom-up tabulation usually fills the whole table.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: memoization is lazy, tabulation is systematic.

options.text: False
options.why: Both are valid DP, but memoization is the lazy one that skips unreachable states.

questions.explanation: Memoization is easier to write from the recurrence but can hit recursion depth limits; tabulation avoids recursion and often allows space reduction, such as keeping only the previous row.

questions.prompt: What is the tight time complexity of generating all subsets of n distinct numbers by backtracking, when each subset is copied into the result list?

options.text: O(2^n): there are 2^n subsets and copying each one is free.
options.why: Copying a subset costs up to n, so the total is larger.

options.text: O(n * 2^n): 2^n subsets, copying each costs up to n.
options.why: Right: the copy cost multiplies the number of subsets.

options.text: O(n!): every ordering of the elements is generated.
options.why: That fits permutations; subsets ignore order.

options.text: O(n^2): each element is paired with every other element.
options.why: Subsets are not limited to pairs; their number is exponential.

questions.explanation: Permutations of n items are O(n * n!). Pruning (for example sorting candidates in combination sum and stopping when a candidate exceeds the remaining target) cuts branches but usually does not change the worst-case bound.

questions.prompt: Select all habits that help in a timed mock coding interview.

options.text: Explain your approach out loud before coding and keep narrating while you work.
options.why: Right: the interviewer can only grade and help with what they hear.

options.text: Write your own test cases, including empty and single-element inputs, and run one by hand.
options.why: Right: a dry run catches off-by-one and base-case bugs.

options.text: State the time and space complexity yourself without waiting to be asked.
options.why: Right: it shows you evaluate your own solution.

options.text: Stay silent until the code compiles, then explain it all at the end.
options.why: Silence leaves no chance for hints and hides your reasoning.

options.text: Skip the brute force and code only the optimal answer to save time.
options.why: A brute force is a safe baseline and the path to the better idea.

questions.explanation: If you are stuck, say what you have tried and what you are considering, and ask for a hint. A working suboptimal solution beats a half-written optimal one.
